Abstract

We study Bedford–Taylor products in the original Chambert–Loir–Ducros calculus over a fixed finite extension of Qp\mathbf Q_pQp​. A symmetric middle-positive current, separately closed for d′d'd′ and d′′d''d′′, is retained as the background. Locally bounded classical plurisubharmonic potentials give intrinsic mixed currents with weighted joint decreasing continuity. The kernel of curvature on bounded classical differences yields a potential-independent operation, and continuous coefficient relations extend it to a module of curvature currents. An order estimate then gives a faithful completion of that module inside the original currents. On strict Laurent domains whose closed boxes carry the background, the relative first-energy calculus admits a complete Borel realization with critical weighted continuity. We describe its variational source map and prove that a single geometric potential detects the entire original-test defect of a literal Radon datum. In remaining degree one, finite signed energy-diffuse data have a unique relative renormalized zero-boundary solution. The regularization and analytic energy estimates used in the constructions are stated with their precise hypotheses and cited to the accompanying foundational manuscripts.

1 Introduction

The Bedford–Taylor recursion differentiates a potential after multiplying it by a positive closed current. Over a non-Archimedean field, this construction raises two distinct questions. The first is analytic: which potential classes make the recursive products positive and stable under approximation? The second concerns the objects on which the construction depends: when can a potential be replaced by another potential with the same curvature, or a finite curvature expression by another expression representing the same current?

We develop these questions with one positive closed current retained as the background. The resulting local calculus leads to an ordered module of curvature currents. On specified analytic domains it also leads to relative capacities, a complete first-energy space, and source equations. The proofs use the local regularization of classical potentials and the analytic energy estimates in the accompanying manuscripts [Cont, Bound, Order, Energy, Dual]. The arguments below give the constructions and the transitions between these theories; the cited analytic inputs are stated at the points where they enter.

Proof in Section 3.

Coefficient multiplication and the ordered construction are established in Section 2. The convergence proof uses a common collar on a small norm box. The collar permits Green exchange with a smooth argument before any two discontinuous approximation parameters are passed to a limit. Positivity then gives a lower bound for a fixed trace test. A separate upper bound for decreasing weights determines the trace limit and hence all original test limits. The final curvature-independence assertion is proved in Section 4.

The probe is a convergent sum of exact-moment compensators. Its selected summands admit both signs of a prescribed compact smooth direction. The normal inequality on these two competitors gives the defect bound; literal integration then turns equality on all tests into equality of Radon measures.

1.4 Relation to the existing calculus

The recursive construction and continuous-potential theory originate in [CLD12, §5.6]. The revised treatment [CLD25, Lemma 8.5.5 and Propositions 8.7.2, 8.7.4] supplies positivity, local uniform stability and symmetry for continuous psh potentials on a positive closed background. Its discussion [CLD25, §8.6.1–8.6.2] isolates the question of annihilating zero-curvature potential differences against a background. The regularization manuscripts [Cont, Bound] supply the particular continuous and locally bounded classical approximation statements used here. The bounded curvature quotient and ordered difference criterion are developed in [Quot, Order].

The relative energy construction in [Energy] works with the original coefficient measures and the full local test sheaf. Its global boundary class is tied to (1.6). The dual construction in [Dual] then treats a source as a literal measure when measure equality is required. This separation of local products, relative completion and source compatibility determines the organization of the present article.

Wu [Wu26, Theorem 4.2 and Appendix A] constructs top-degree local Monge–Ampère measures for a class defined by decreasing tropical-convex PL approximation on a fixed neighborhood. The classical regularization input here supplies that neighborhood and approximation from the complete-extension curve definition; the background calculus retains all allowed bidegrees. On balanced polyhedral and tropical spaces, [BMPS26, APW26] develop related product, energy and source theories. Their geometric categories provide useful comparison for the relation and solvability questions arising from original analytic currents.

Relative capacity with a positive closed current is classical in the complex setting [DE06]. Relative non-pluripolar products and their closedness are developed in [Vu21, Theorem 3.7], and the constant-one first-energy mixed inequality has the complex precedent [Ceg98, Theorem 3.2]. The role of these constructions here is their realization with the fixed original non-Archimedean background, coefficient measures and boundary class.

General renormalized measure-data equations for transient regular Dirichlet forms satisfying the strong sector condition are treated in [KR15]. In the linear part of this article, the analytic work is the faithful realization of the part form, its measures and its scalar chain identities in the original CLD calculus. The abstract finite-energy nest theorem used there is [KR17, Lemma 2.1].

2 Coefficient measures and the ordered construction

2.1 Positive currents and analytic-space coefficients

A current is of coefficient Radon type if its coefficient functionals in every finite original moment presentation are signed Radon measures on the analytic domain, compatibly with scalar multiplication, relations between forms, and common refinements. In particular, for every compact original test η\etaη there is a signed measure μT,η\mu_{T,\eta}μT,η​ satisfying ∫a dμT,η=⟨T,aη⟩(a original smooth).\int a\,d\mu_{T,\eta}=\langle T,a\eta\rangle \quad(a\text{ original smooth}).∫adμT,η​=⟨T,aη⟩(a original smooth). This condition permits the definition

⟨hT,η⟩=∫h dμT,η(2.1)\langle hT,\eta\rangle=\int h\,d\mu_{T,\eta} \tag{2.1}⟨hT,η⟩=∫hdμT,η​(2.1)

for an actual locally bounded Borel function hhh.

Lemma 2.1 (Finite test control). Every positive current is of coefficient Radon type. For each compact original test η\etaη there is a nonnegative compact trace test Θ\ThetaΘ and a constant cηc_\etacη​ such that

∣⟨T,hη⟩∣≤cη∥h∥∞⟨T,Θ⟩(2.2)|\langle T,h\eta\rangle| \le c_\eta\|h\|_\infty\langle T,\Theta\rangle \tag{2.2}∣⟨T,hη⟩∣≤cη​∥h∥∞​⟨T,Θ⟩(2.2)

for positive TTT and bounded Borel hhh on the chosen compact stage. The positive cone is weakly closed and pointed. If positive currents TjT_jTj​ converge on all original tests, their coefficient variations are uniformly bounded on each compact stage. Thus fjTj→fTf_jT_j\to fTfj​Tj​→fT for locally uniformly convergent continuous fj→ff_j\to ffj​→f.

Proof. Localize to a finite moment presentation containing the coefficients of η\etaη and a smooth cutoff χ\chiχ equal to one near its support. A positive current annihilates the antisymmetric part of a test. For the symmetric part, put β=∑a=1Nd′ta∧d′′ta,Ω=βm/m!,\beta=\sum_{a=1}^N d't_a\wedge d''t_a, \qquad\Omega=\beta^m/m!,β=a=1∑N​d′ta​∧d′′ta​,Ω=βm/m!, where (m,m)(m,m)(m,m) is the test bidegree. The coefficient matrix of Ω\OmegaΩ is positive definite on this finite exterior space. Matrix domination therefore gives cη∥h∥∞χΩ±hη≥0c_\eta\|h\|_\infty\chi\Omega\pm h\eta\ge0cη​∥h∥∞​χΩ±hη≥0 for smooth hhh. The inequality persists after adjoining scalar moments and pulling back to a common refinement. Positivity proves (2.2) for smooth hhh.

Compact uniform density of original smooth scalar functions and the Riesz representation theorem produce the coefficient measures. Their uniqueness preserves the original relations and refinements. Bounded Borel approximation against these measures gives (2.2) in the stated form. If Tj→TT_j\to TTj​→T, the trace masses ⟨Tj,Θ⟩\langle T_j,\Theta\rangle⟨Tj​,Θ⟩ are bounded, so the same coefficient estimate is uniform. Approximate fff uniformly by a smooth function, pass the fixed smooth pairing, and then let the uniform error go to zero; the term (fj−f)Tj(f_j-f)T_j(fj​−f)Tj​ is controlled by the same bound. Closedness of the positive cone follows on each positive test. If both TTT and −T-T−T are positive, the trace control makes every pairing zero. This is the coefficient argument of [Cont, Lemma Continuous coefficients] in the present analytic category, using the ordinary local transport of [Bound]. ◻

2.2 Regularization on a fixed neighborhood

We use the following two precise regularization consequences. The first is [Bound, Theorem 1.5]; its construction uses the prescribed field and the original calibration.

Proposition 2.2 (Classical regularization). For every u∈Cb(U)u\in\mathcal C_b(U)u∈Cb​(U) and every x∈Ux\in Ux∈U there is one ordinary neighborhood WWW of xxx and continuous semipositive rational PL functions pjp_jpj​ over KKK, defined on WWW, with pj↓up_j\downarrow upj​↓u. The class Cb\mathcal C_bCb​ is stable under decreasing locally bounded limits. For finitely many decreasing families with locally bounded endpoints, the common projective extension construction gives one such neighborhood for all rows. Continuous members of these rows admit smooth positive uniform approximants on smaller fixed neighborhoods. Smooth majorants of each bounded member can consequently be chosen pointwise convergent and locally uniformly bounded.

The simultaneous neighborhood assertion uses the norm-box projective extension in [Bound, Appendix D]. Smooth approximation of the continuous rows is [Cont, Lemma Smooth approximation of FS metrics and Proposition Regularized maximum]. The smooth approximating rows in the last sentence are not required to decrease. Their precise collar version is proved below.

Proposition 2.3 (First order and ordered products). If RRR is a background and u∈Cbu\in\mathcal C_bu∈Cb​, then D(uR)D(uR)D(uR) is positive, symmetric, separately closed and of coefficient Radon type. Iterating this operation defines (1.1). The ordered products are local and separately additive and positively homogeneous in the potentials. They are independent of the approximants used in the first-order construction.

Proof. Work on a regularization neighborhood and choose continuous positive pj↓up_j\downarrow upj​↓u. The continuous background theorem [Cont, Theorem Continuous potentials on a positive closed background], transported to this neighborhood as in [Bound], makes D(pjR)D(p_jR)D(pj​R) positive. Bounded convergence against the fixed coefficient measures of RRR gives pjR→uRp_jR\to uRpj​R→uR on every original test. Distributional differentiation gives D(pjR)→D(uR)D(p_jR)\to D(uR)D(pj​R)→D(uR). Positivity and symmetry pass to the limit. The identities d′D=d′′D=0d'D=d''D=0d′D=d′′D=0 give separate closedness, and lemma 2.1 gives coefficient Radon type. The result is the derivative of the already defined actual product uRuRuR, so it is independent of the row. The same argument applies successively to every positive closed intermediate current. Linearity of multiplication and differentiation gives the algebraic properties; restriction commutes with both operations. ◻

Proposition 2.4 (Relative local mass estimate). Fix compact test stages L⋐WL\Subset WL⋐W and k≤qk\le qk≤q. For each finite original coefficient presentation on LLL there is a constant CCC and a compact positive trace test Θ\ThetaΘ on WWW such that ∥TS,k(u1,…,uk)∥L≤C∏i=1k∥ui∥L∞(W)⟨S,Θ⟩\|T_{S,k}(u_1,\ldots,u_k)\|_{L} \le C\prod_{i=1}^k\|u_i\|_{L^\infty(W)} \langle S,\Theta\rangle∥TS,k​(u1​,…,uk​)∥L​≤Ci=1∏k​∥ui​∥L∞(W)​⟨S,Θ⟩ whenever the displayed bounds are finite. Here the left side denotes the sum of the coefficient variations in that finite presentation. The estimate is local and may be applied after every actual refinement.

Proof. Choose nested compactly supported cutoffs between LLL and WWW and add the finitely many moment coordinates used by their coefficients. The trace estimate in lemma 2.1 reduces a coefficient variation to a positive trace pairing. For one differentiated slot, distributional integration by parts writes it as ⟨u1R,D(χα)⟩\langle u_1R,D(\chi\alpha)\rangle⟨u1​R,D(χα)⟩, where α\alphaα is a fixed closed trace form. On its compact support both signs of D(χα)D(\chi\alpha)D(χα) are bounded by a constant times the next positive trace form. The coefficient bound is therefore at most C∥u1∥∞C\|u_1\|_\inftyC∥u1​∥∞​ times the trace mass of RRR on the next compact stage. Repeat with the remaining differentiated slots. The last trace is a fixed compact test against SSS. This proves the estimate; finite localization supplies the general compact stage. ◻

4 The curvature quotient of bounded classical potentials

Theorem 4.1 (The bounded-difference criterion). For h∈DSHlb(U)h\in\mathscr{DSH}_{\mathrm{lb}}(U)h∈DSHlb​(U), D[h]≥0⟺h∈Cb(U).D[h]\ge0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad h\in\mathcal C_b(U).D[h]≥0⟺h∈Cb​(U). Both sides concern the given actual function.

We recall the two geometric steps behind the criterion, since its use is stronger than a choice of a good representative for a distribution. Order transfer along analytic curve maps after every complete extension preserves the actual bounded classical difference and the original curvature inequality. On a curve the positive difference of the two Laplacians gives an actual subharmonic difference: positive Green potentials identify its endpoint values along nested discs. To recover ambient upper semicontinuity, use a compact semistable cover of a norm box and its finite Shilov interpolants. If h=a−bh=a-bh=a−b and a<a(x)+ϵa<a(x)+\epsilona<a(x)+ϵ on the box, the one-sided curve maximum principle gives h∘q≤Phh\circ q\le P hh∘q≤Ph and b∘q≤Pbb\circ q\le P bb∘q≤Pb on each compact chart. The fiber maximum of the continuous function PhP hPh is upper semicontinuous and majorizes hhh, while its value above xxx is at most h(x)+ϵh(x)+\epsilonh(x)+ϵ. Letting ϵ\epsilonϵ decrease proves ambient upper semicontinuity. The full complete-extension curve condition then gives classical psh membership. These steps and the required algebraic localization and trace arguments are proved in [Order, Sections 19–21]; the zero-curvature predecessor appears in [Quot, Section 10].

The individual restricted stages in (7.1) may have boundary derivatives; the closedness theorem concerns their locally finite limit. The exact sources of theorem 7.2 are [Energy, Sections 8, 12, 15–20, 31]. In particular, the first-order estimate is (FO8), the curvature and energy bounds are (PG3) and (PG12), and the bounded Borel construction is the lemma Analytic bounded capacitary calculus. The boundary comparison and all-degree capacity estimates also give the following consequences used below: equality of two no-loss top measures implies equality of their potentials modulo local outer capacity; the actual power classes are closed under finite sums and maxima; and capacity convergence of uniformly energy-bounded tuples passes bounded weighted products below the critical degree. These are proved in [Energy, Sections 12, 14–18, 28].

8.2 The Borel class and its intrinsic original currents

Definition 8.2 (Strong relative first-energy completion). Let E^str1(V)\widehat{\mathcal E}^1_{\rm str}(V)Estr1​(V) consist of actual Borel functions u:V→[−∞,0]u:V\to[-\infty,0]u:V→[−∞,0] which are limits of an actual strongly Cauchy row in every local truncated outer SSS-capacity. Equality means local outer-capacity equality. The capacities may equivalently be taken on all compact cores in the fixed domain VVV, by the analytic capacity-domain comparison in theorem 7.2. A choice of actual defining row is not part of the element of this quotient.

Proposition 8.3 (Borel limits of all strongly Cauchy actual rows). Every row satisfying (8.1) has a limit in definition 8.2, unique modulo local outer-capacity zero. Every member of that space is finite and continuous locally outside ordinary open sets of arbitrarily small outer capacity. Its pole set is locally outer-capacity zero.

Proof. Uniform energy and (7.13) make each fixed bounded truncation of the row Cauchy in every local outer capacity. Apply the countable compact-core and integer-level diagonal construction from the bounded completion. A subsequence has compatible pointwise limits of all bounded truncations off a locally outer-null set. Its actual pointwise limsup defines a Borel u≤0u\leq0u≤0 on all of VVV, and the Cauchy property gives the required capacity convergence for the full row.

There is a uniform deep sublevel estimate. The no-loss sublevel inequality and the first-energy bound imply

CS({uj<−R};V)≤CqMR−d.(8.9)C_S(\{u_j<-R\};V)\leq C_q M R^{-d}. \tag{8.9}CS​({uj​<−R};V)≤Cq​MR−d.(8.9)

These sets are ordinary open, so the same bound holds for their outer capacities. On a fixed compact core, the set {u<−2R}\{u<-2R\}{u<−2R} is contained in {uj<−R}\{u_j<-R\}{uj​<−R} together with a positive gap of the fixed truncations at 3R3R3R. Pass j→∞j\to\inftyj→∞ in the outer-capacity subadditivity bound. It follows that the pole of uuu has outer capacity zero on that core. Outside an ordinary open cover of a sufficiently deep sublevel, uuu agrees with one bounded truncation. Its bounded-completion quasicontinuity then proves the stated finite local quasicontinuity. The level-set triangle inequality proves uniqueness. ◻

inf⁡L≥1{Lbs+Lb−dΦ(L/4)}⟶0(s↓0).(8.16)\inf_{L\geq1}\{L^b s+L^{b-d}\Phi(L/4)\} \longrightarrow0\quad(s\downarrow0). \tag{8.16}L≥1inf​{Lbs+Lb−dΦ(L/4)}⟶0(s↓0).(8.16)

Its weak-limit proof keeps LLL fixed until after ordinary-open variation lower semicontinuity and Radon outer regularity. Thus it controls both the defining and limiting coefficients, including the critical case b=db=db=d. It annihilates every locally outer-null set and, in particular, the joint pole set. The bounded quasicontinuous multiplier argument therefore passes every bounded continuous function of a fixed clipped tuple.

For endpoint integrability apply that argument to θR(z)min⁡((1+z)a,H)\theta_R(z)\min((1+z)^a,H)θR​(z)min((1+z)a,H), where z=−∑iuiz=-\sum_i u_iz=−∑i​ui​ and θR\theta_RθR​ is zero below RRR and one above 2R2R2R. Passing to the bounded multiplier limit and then H↑∞H\uparrow\inftyH↑∞ proves the same tail bound for the limiting positive traces. Variation lower semicontinuity handles signed first-order coefficients, and positive diagonal controls handle cross energies. Adding the bounded-value part gives actual coefficient integrability. Clipping a general FFF and then letting its clipping level tend to infinity proves (8.11). Consequently all multipliers in (8.12) and (7.4) are defined before distributional differentiation, and the original row identities pass to the limit.

For two different defining tuples with the same Borel capacity limits, their bounded completed stages are identical. The union of their finitely many row families has the same vanishing-tail property. The preceding construction therefore gives identical unbounded currents and actual multipliers. This proves approximation independence.

Finally, (8.11) gives local convergence of (8.3). The uniform global tightness in lemma 8.1, together with the uniform finite mixed-energy bound (7.9), identifies a finite global limiting measure and gives its total-mass convergence. This is precisely (8.13). Tightness also passes every bounded original scalar test. The independent-index assertions follow from the same bounds, or by applying the argument to every sequence of independently diverging indices. ◻

8.3 Intrinsic discrepancy and completeness

Define on this Borel space

Lemma 8.5 (Uniform discrepancy continuity on energy balls). The completed space is closed under finite sums and nonnegative scalar multiples. Its mixed energy is symmetric, positive and multilinear on that cone, and satisfies the constant-one Hölder inequality. The assertion at M=0M=0M=0 means that both sides are zero.

Proof. For two strongly Cauchy defining rows, the sum rows have the required Borel capacity limit. Expand the discrepancy of two independently late sum rows into finitely many global mixed energies. Equation (8.13) makes each term converge to the corresponding completed mixed energy; the total limiting discrepancy is zero. Thus the sum row is strongly Cauchy. Positive scaling is immediate, and zero scaling means the zero function even at poles. Passing the actual finite mixed identities and (7.9) through (8.13) now proves all asserted cone identities.

The actual inequalities (7.12), (7.14), and (7.17) pass by global mixed-energy convergence. For (7.12), its left side is the actual weight ∣u−v∣|u-v|∣u−v∣, which has degree-one growth and is bounded by (−u)+(−v)(-u)+(-v)(−u)+(−v); (8.11) and the tightness of these two critical positive mixed measures pass its global integral. For (7.13), use defining rows, their convergent energies, and the level-set triangle inequality for clipped gaps; then remove deep sublevels using (8.9) and decrease the intermediate gap threshold. This also proves that I^=0\widehat I=0I=0 gives equality in all local outer capacities. The converse follows from intrinsic current and multiplier independence.

It remains to prove (8.18). It suffices first to consider actual potentials. Write h=a−a′h=a-a'h=a−a′. Strongly convergent finite tuples have every original local weighted-current limit in (8.11), including all its critical endpoints, and the global mixed-energy and weighted-measure limits (8.13). The weighted limits here are original-current limits.

Proof. If (vl)(v_l)(vl​) is an actual defining row for a completed uuu, then for fixed lll, (8.13) gives I^(vl,u)=lim⁡r→∞I(vl,vr)\widehat I(v_l,u)=\lim_{r\to\infty}I(v_l,v_r)I(vl​,u)=limr→∞​I(vl​,vr​). Now let (uj)(u_j)(uj​) be completed and I^\widehat II-Cauchy. The energy-root estimate bounds its energies. Choose actual vjv_jvj​ with I^(vj,uj)<2−j\widehat I(v_j,u_j)<2^{-j}I(vj​,uj​)<2−j and uniformly bounded energies. Applying (8.18) in its two slots shows

The forward implication of (8.20) follows from the completed energy-root and capacity estimates. For the reverse, the energies are uniformly bounded. Bounded completed stages and the strict subcritical truncation bound for top unweighted currents give local convergence of their top measures. More explicitly, the stage error has order at most CM/LC M/LCM/L for degree q<dq<dq<d; first fix LLL, use bounded-completion capacity continuity, and then let LLL grow. lim inf⁡jB^(uj,u[q])≥e^(u),lim inf⁡jB^(u,uj[q])≥e^(u).(8.22)\liminf_j\widehat B(u_j,u^{[q]})\geq\widehat e(u),\qquad \liminf_j\widehat B(u,u_j^{[q]})\geq\widehat e(u). \tag{8.22}jliminf​B(uj​,u[q])≥e(u),jliminf​B(u,uj[q]​)≥e(u).(8.22)

Hölder gives upper bounds tending to e^(u)\widehat e(u)e(u) for both cross energies. Expanding (8.17) proves the converse. This argument uses no critical weighted continuity to prove that very continuity.

For a strongly convergent completed tuple choose, at the jjjth row, classical approximants with discrepancy at most 2−j2^{-j}2−j, and sufficiently accurate values on the first jjj compact test stages and bounded clipped weights. The defining-row convergence allows these finitely many requirements simultaneously. By (8.18), these actual rows are strongly Cauchy, with the same Borel limits and energies. The preceding construction and (8.11)–(8.13) give the asserted limits. Equivalently, any failure on a fixed test would furnish a subsequence and actual approximants contradicting those already proved actual-row limits. This last argument also covers bounded original scalar tests in the global statement. ◻

8.4 Monotone closure and the capacity integral

Proposition 8.7 (Monotone closure). For completed potentials a≤ba\le ba≤b relatively quasi-everywhere, 0≤I^(a,b)≤e^(a)−e^(b).0\le\widehat I(a,b)\le\widehat e(a)-\widehat e(b).0≤I(a,b)≤e(a)−e(b). An increasing sequence in the strong cone converges strongly to its pointwise monotone Borel limit. The same holds for a decreasing sequence with uniformly bounded energies. Equalities and monotonicity are understood outside one locally outer-null set.

Proof. The mixed energy is decreasing in each potential for pointwise order: this follows from positivity in the weight slot and symmetry in every other slot. Both cross terms in the discrepancy are consequently at least e^(b)\widehat e(b)e(b), proving the inequality. Along an increasing sequence the energies decrease and are nonnegative; along a decreasing sequence they increase and are bounded by hypothesis. In either case they converge, so the displayed inequality makes the row strongly Cauchy. Completeness supplies a limit. A summable-capacity diagonal subsequence of its bounded truncations converges pointwise off a locally outer-null set; monotonicity identifies this limit with the specified Borel monotone limit. Thus the full sequence converges strongly. ◻

We also use the following precise capacity characterization from [Energy, Theorem 37.2]. A Borel function u≤0u\le0u≤0 represents a member of the strong cone if and only if each u(m)u^{(m)}u(m) is a bounded capacitary limit of actual classical functions on the same domain VVV with values in [−m,0][-m,0][−m,0], and

The admissibility of the bounded stages is part of this criterion. The completed sublevel theorem in [Energy, Section 36] proves the capacity inequalities and the forward direction. For the reverse, form vj=max⁡(u,jρ)=max⁡(u(j),jρ)v_j=\max(u,j\rho)=\max(u^{(j)},j\rho)vj​=max(u,jρ)=max(u(j),jρ). Bounded classical approximants of u(j)u^{(j)}u(j), followed by this maximum, are bounded below by the actual first-energy barrier jρj\rhojρ. The fixed-barrier critical convergence of theorem 7.2 makes their limit a strong member vjv_jvj​. The sublevel bounds give e^(vj)≤2dJ1∗(u)\widehat e(v_j)\le2^dJ_1^*(u)e(vj​)≤2dJ1∗​(u). The vjv_jvj​ decrease, hence converge strongly by proposition 8.7. On a compact core and for fixed RRR, strict negativity of ρ\rhoρ gives vj(R)=u(R)v_j^{(R)}=u^{(R)}vj(R)​=u(R) for all large jjj. The completed limit is therefore the given capacity class of uuu. The sublevel theorem then gives both inequalities in (8.23).

ΓS(Tkuj,Tluj)⟶ΓS(Tku,Tlu).(10.30)\Gamma_S(T_ku_j,T_lu_j) \longrightarrow\Gamma_S(T_ku,T_lu). \tag{10.30}ΓS​(Tk​uj​,Tl​uj​)⟶ΓS​(Tk​u,Tl​u).(10.30)

If Φ∈C2(R)\Phi\in C^2(\mathbf R)Φ∈C2(R) has bounded first derivative and compactly supported second derivative, then

D(Φ(uj)S)⟶D(Φ(u)S)in global total variation.(10.31)D(\Phi(u_j)S)\longrightarrow D(\Phi(u)S) \quad\hbox{in global total variation}. \tag{10.31}D(Φ(uj​)S)⟶D(Φ(u)S)in global total variation.(10.31)

If, more restrictively, Φ′\Phi'Φ′ has compact support, then Φ(uj)−Φ(0)→Φ(u)−Φ(0)\Phi(u_j)-\Phi(0)\to\Phi(u)-\Phi(0)Φ(uj​)−Φ(0)→Φ(u)−Φ(0) strongly in HHH. For this latter class both original first-order currents d′(Φ(uj)S)d'(\Phi(u_j)S)d′(Φ(uj​)S) and d′′(Φ(uj)S)d''(\Phi(u_j)S)d′′(Φ(uj​)S) converge in local coefficient total variation, against every original compact complementary smooth test and every actual moment refinement. The zero-order multipliers Φ(uj)S\Phi(u_j)SΦ(uj​)S converge in that same local coefficient sense under the hypotheses of (10.31).

Proof. The finite-datum estimates give uj→uu_j\to uuj​→u in energy capacity and in L1(λ)L^1(\lambda)L1(λ). The clipped functions converge in L2(λ)L^2(\lambda)L2(λ): they are bounded by kkk, and λ(F)<∞\lambda(F)<\inftyλ(F)<∞ because the part domain is relatively compact in the neighborhood where λ\lambdaλ is Radon. Also E(Tkuj)≤k∥μj∥TV\mathcal E(T_ku_j)\leq k\|\mu_j\|_{\rm TV}E(Tk​uj​)≤k∥μj​∥TV​, so these vectors are bounded in HHH. Every weakly convergent subsequence therefore has the unique L2L^2L2 representative TkuT_kuTk​u. Consequently the whole sequence converges weakly in HHH.

Take a=0,b=ka=0,b=ka=0,b=k in (10.20). The exact norm identity is

E(Tkuj)=−∫FTku~j dμj,E(Tku)=−∫FTku~ dμ.(10.32)\mathcal E(T_ku_j)=-\int_F T_k\widetilde u_j\,d\mu_j, \qquad \mathcal E(T_ku)=-\int_F T_k\widetilde u\,d\mu. \tag{10.32}E(Tk​uj​)=−∫F​Tk​uj​dμj​,E(Tk​u)=−∫F​Tk​udμ.(10.32)

The difference between the first datum integral and the second is bounded in absolute value by

k∥μj−μ∥TV+∫F∣Tku~j−Tku~∣ d∣μ∣.(10.33)k\|\mu_j-\mu\|_{\rm TV} +\int_F|T_k\widetilde u_j-T_k\widetilde u|\,d|\mu|. \tag{10.33}k∥μj​−μ∥TV​+∫F​∣Tk​uj​−Tk​u∣d∣μ∣.(10.33)

The second term tends to zero by energy-capacity convergence, finite diffuseness of ∣μ∣|\mu|∣μ∣, and boundedness of the clippings. Thus the norms in (10.32) converge. Weak convergence and convergence of norms in the Hilbert space prove (10.29). The exact band identity is what turns weak clipping convergence into norm convergence.

The original closed gradient module gives, for fj,gj,f,g∈Hf_j,g_j,f,g\in Hfj​,gj​,f,g∈H,

∥ΓS(fj,gj)−ΓS(f,g)∥TV≤∥fj−f∥H∥gj∥H+∥f∥H∥gj−g∥H.(10.34)\|\Gamma_S(f_j,g_j)-\Gamma_S(f,g)\|_{\rm TV} \leq \|f_j-f\|_H\|g_j\|_H +\|f\|_H\|g_j-g\|_H. \tag{10.34}∥ΓS​(fj​,gj​)−ΓS​(f,g)∥TV​≤∥fj​−f∥H​∥gj​∥H​+∥f∥H​∥gj​−g∥H​.(10.34)

This is measure Cauchy–Schwarz after adding and subtracting ΓS(f,gj)\Gamma_S(f,g_j)ΓS​(f,gj​). Applying (10.29) proves (10.30).

For (10.31), choose MMM larger than the support radius of Φ′′\Phi''Φ′′. The all-original chain identity reads

D(Φ(uj)S)=Φ′(u~j)μj+Φ′′(u~j)ΓS(TMuj).(10.35)D(\Phi(u_j)S)=\Phi'(\widetilde u_j)\mu_j +\Phi''(\widetilde u_j)\Gamma_S(T_Mu_j). \tag{10.35}D(Φ(uj​)S)=Φ′(uj​)μj​+Φ′′(uj​)ΓS​(TM​uj​).(10.35)

The first term converges in variation: its changing-datum error is at most ∥Φ′∥∞∥μj−μ∥TV\|\Phi'\|_\infty\|\mu_j-\mu\|_{\rm TV}∥Φ′∥∞​∥μj​−μ∥TV​, and its fixed-datum multiplier error tends to zero by finite diffuseness and capacity convergence. For the second term use (10.30) and then bounded convergence in measure against the fixed finite diffuse measure ΓS(TMu)\Gamma_S(T_Mu)ΓS​(TM​u). This gives its variation convergence as well and proves (10.31). The zero-order multiplier claim follows from the Lipschitz bound for Φ\PhiΦ, L1(λ)L^1(\lambda)L1(λ) stability and the faithful original coefficient domination.

If Φ′\Phi'Φ′ has compact support, its normalized composition is a smooth function of one sufficiently large clipping. The closed gradient formula and (10.29) give strong convergence: the changing-gradient term is bounded by ∥Φ′∥∞∥TMuj−TMu∥H\|\Phi'\|_\infty\|T_Mu_j-T_Mu\|_H∥Φ′∥∞​∥TM​uj​−TM​u∥H​, and the changing scalar factor tends to zero in the fixed finite energy measure. Its L2L^2L2 representative converges by the same bounded composition argument. Finally, on a fixed original compact stage, write any complementary one-form test as a finite sum of bounded smooth coefficients times differentials of original local moment functions. Multiply those moment functions by original compact cutoffs equal to one on the test support. The coefficient pairing of a first-order derivative with each such term is an original mixed gradient measure; (10.34), or its one-variable Cauchy–Schwarz bound, controls its variation by a fixed constant times the HHH-norm of the changing potential. This proves local coefficient-TV convergence of both first-order currents. The argument starts with an arbitrary original test and is valid after any further actual moment refinement. ◻
